summary: Nuno Campos (Witan Labs) describes a 4-month project to make coding agents proficient at spreadsheets, targeting parity with their performance in Python or JavaScript. Spreadsheets are deceptively hard for LLMs because the visual structure humans perceive—revenue tables, assumptions, charts, formatting—is invisible to a language model. The team began at approximately 50% accuracy on a financial analysis benchmark. Early approaches failed: a three-agent architecture (discovery, edit, verification) was too rigid—discovery ran once upfront with no revisiting, and context did not flow between agents. Multiple spreadsheet representations (SQL, XML, CSV/TSV, HTML) were tried; none sufficed standalone, though CSV/TSV views and HTML rendering became useful components within the final system. The biggest breakthrough was consolidating roughly 15 separate tools into a single Node.js REPL with persistent state across calls, enabling agents to combine operations in one invocation and reason incrementally. The actual spreadsheet manipulation runs in C#, leveraging each language's strengths. This reduced typical 10-15 sequential tool calls that frequently timed out to a single combined call, eliminating timeouts. Agents using a REPL wrote shorter scripts with more interleaved reasoning. Adding new capabilities simply required adding TypeScript type definitions to the prompt. Accuracy improved from 50% to 74% after the REPL, then to 92% through incremental changes—better fuzzy search, formula dependency tracing, prompt improvements, and bug fixes. A high-fidelity verification loop, powered by a formula engine and a render engine producing images of spreadsheet ranges, was essential; incomplete implementations produced worse results because agents trusted incorrect computations. Domain knowledge in prompts survived all architecture iterations, consistently improving results by focusing the model on task-relevant concepts. Evaluation started with LLM-as-judge but was supplemented with deterministic comparisons using golden spreadsheets as black-box test cases—feeding known inputs into both reference and model-produced spreadsheets and comparing outputs. Many apparent reasoning failures turned out to be infrastructure bugs—bugs in code, prompts with wrong examples the model faithfully followed, or tool failures causing retries. Six generalizable lessons emerged: give agents real scripting languages instead of many tool calls; build feedback loops even when they require custom engines; invest in choosing the right interface and expect to revisit it as models evolve; value planning and thinking before acting; use domain knowledge prompts to focus attention; and prefer deterministic evaluation while using LLM-as-judge when necessary, always checking traces for hidden bugs.

sections.title: Introduction: The Spreadsheet Challenge for AI
sections.summary: Nuno introduces the 4-month project to make coding agents as good at spreadsheets as at Python or JavaScript. Spreadsheets are deceptively hard for LLMs because the visual structure humans perceive instantly is invisible to models, requiring disambiguation of revenue types, quarters, and distinguishing inputs from formulas.

sections.title: Dead End: Three-Agent Architecture
sections.summary: A three-agent architecture (discovery, edit with a five-step process, verify) changed the nature of errors from execution mistakes to planning mistakes, which were easier to rectify. However, the design was too rigid: discovery ran once upfront with no revisiting, and context did not flow between agents.

sections.title: Dead Ends: Spreadsheet Representation Formats
sections.summary: The team tried every conceivable way to represent spreadsheets to an LLM. SQL was familiar to models but did not work; XML (Excel's native format) also failed. CSV/TSV views and HTML rendering, while insufficient standalone, became useful components within the final REPL-based system, with HTML leading to a rendering engine for visual output.

sections.title: Breakthrough: Consolidating Tools into a Node.js REPL
sections.summary: The biggest breakthrough was replacing ~15 accumulated tools with a single Node.js REPL. All prior tools became JavaScript functions the agent could combine in one call. JavaScript was chosen for sandboxing ease and LLM familiarity; actual spreadsheet manipulation runs in C#, leveraging each language's strengths.

sections.title: Before/After Comparison and REPL vs Code Mode
sections.summary: Before the REPL, agents made 10-15 sequential tool calls that often timed out. After, they combined operations in a single call. The REPL goes beyond basic code mode by maintaining persistent state across calls, enabling incremental reasoning. Agents wrote shorter scripts with more interleaved reasoning, reaching better answers faster. Adding new methods only requires TypeScript type definitions in the prompt.

sections.title: Results: 50% to 92% Accuracy
sections.summary: Accuracy went from 50% to 74% after the REPL, then to 92% through incremental improvements including better fuzzy search, formula tracing, system prompt improvements, and bug fixes. The REPL approach also eliminated the 5-minute timeout problem entirely.

sections.title: Verification Loop and High-Fidelity Engines
sections.summary: Drawing parallels to coding agents that compile and test, the team built a formula engine and a render engine to close the feedback loop. These engines must be high fidelity—an incomplete engine implementing only 50% of Excel formulas produces worse results because agents trust incorrect computations. The REPL is the interface; the verification loop is the durable part that benefits from more capable models.

sections.title: Domain Knowledge Prompting and Evaluation
sections.summary: Domain knowledge added to prompts survived all tool iterations and consistently improved results, not because LLMs lack knowledge of terms like revenue or ARR, but because it focuses them on task-relevant concepts. The same prompt worked across different tool architectures. Evaluation was extensive and essential for validating each approach.

sections.title: Evaluation Methodology: From LLM-as-Judge to Deterministic Comparison
sections.summary: The team started with LLM-as-judge for evaluation, which works to some extent but introduces noise—score changes could stem from agent changes or evaluator changes. They replaced it with deterministic comparisons where possible, using golden spreadsheets as black-box tests: feeding known inputs into both the reference and model-produced spreadsheets and comparing outputs.

sections.title: Bugs Masquerading as Reasoning Failures
sections.summary: Many apparent model reasoning failures turned out to be infrastructure bugs—bugs in code, skills, prompts with wrong examples that the model faithfully followed, or tool failures that caused the model to retry and appear confused. Careful trace inspection was essential to distinguish genuine model limitations from fixable bugs.

sections.title: Generalizable Lessons for Other Tasks
sections.summary: Six lessons generalize beyond spreadsheets: (1) if agents make many tool calls, you've invented a bad scripting language—give them a real one; (2) feedback loops matter—build engines if they don't exist; (3) interfaces are critical and should be revisited as models evolve; (4) planning and thinking before acting matters; (5) domain knowledge prompts focus the model on relevant concepts; (6) prefer deterministic evaluation where possible, but use LLM-as-judge when necessary. Always check traces—agent confusion may be bugs.
